Rhythm. Rhythm is the organization of musical time through patterns of duration, pulse, and accent—the element that governs how long notes sound and how they relate to one another and to a steady pulse. Every musical tradition, from Western classical to Indian classical to jazz, has a sophisticated system for organizing rhythm. Rhythm serves as the temporal skeleton on which melody and harmony are built, creating momentum, structure, and expressive power. Rhythm is distinct from beat, the underlying regular pulse, and meter, the recurrent pattern of accented and unaccented beats. Rhythm describes the actual durations of sounding notes against that framework. In Western classical music, rhythm is notated through note values like whole notes, half notes, quarter notes, and rests, organized into measures by a time signature like four four or three four. Syncopation is a disruption of expected rhythmic accent, emphasizing weaker beats or creating patterns that conflict with the underlying meter—a hallmark of jazz, ragtime, and African-influenced musics. In Indian classical music, rhythm is organized by tala, a cyclic rhythmic pattern of fixed duration containing specific beat divisions. The drummer, the tabla player, and melodic soloist must coordinate within the tala framework. Polyrhythm, the simultaneous use of contrasting rhythmic patterns, appears prominently in African and Afro-diasporic musics and has been systematically explored by twentieth-century classical composers. The concept of rhythmic feel or groove—the particular way a rhythm is performed with slight variations in timing and emphasis—is crucial to performance practice in jazz, funk, and contemporary music. Composers such as Igor Stravinsky revolutionized rhythmic complexity in the twentieth century by shifting accents, changing meters abruptly, and creating elaborate polyrhythmic textures.
